items.stem: Define the term 'stare decisis'.
items.answer: Latin for "stand by what has been decided": the principle that courts follow the legal rules decided in earlier cases where the material facts are similar.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: basic/partial definition; 2 marks: full and accurate definition, i.e. latin for "stand by what has been decided": the principle that courts follow the legal rules decided in earlier cases where the material facts are similar. [2]

items.stem: In Patel v Northgate Ltd (fictional, 2021), the Supreme Court held that a landlord was liable for damp caused by a broken gutter. The judge added that "the same principle would probably apply to a free public sports facility". Leila is now bringing a similar case in the county court. Explain which parts of the earlier judgment the county court must follow in Leila's case.
items.answer: Law: the ratio decidendi of a higher court binds lower courts through stare decisis; obiter dicta are persuasive only (R v Howe and R v Gotts); the material facts must be sufficiently similar for the ratio to apply. Application: the Supreme Court is above the county court in the hierarchy; the holding that a landlord was liable for damp caused by a broken gutter is the ratio and binds the county court if the material facts are similar; the remark that "the same principle would probably apply to a free public sports facility" is obiter and need not be followed. Conclusion: The county court is bound by the ratio if the facts are similar but may choose whether to follow the obiter comment.

items.stem: Define the term 'Practice Statement 1966'.
items.answer: A statement by the Lord Chancellor on behalf of the House of Lords that it would treat its own former decisions as normally binding but would depart from them "when it appears right to do so"; it now applies to the Supreme Court.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: basic/partial definition; 2 marks: full and accurate definition, i.e. a statement by the Lord Chancellor on behalf of the House of Lords that it would treat its own former decisions as normally binding but would depart from them "when it appears right to do so"; it now applies to the Supreme Court. There are two earlier Court of Appeal decisions on the same point which were both made without reference to a relevant statute. Advise whether the Court of Appeal is bound by its earlier decisions in Samuel's case. Refer to at least one decided case.
items.answer: Law: the Court of Appeal is normally bound by its own previous decisions (Davis v Johnson 1979); Young v Bristol Aeroplane (1944): exceptions for conflicting decisions, conflict with a later House of Lords/Supreme Court decision and per incuriam decisions; the Practice Statement does not apply to the Court of Appeal. Application: the earlier decisions were both made without reference to a relevant statute; so the decisions were made per incuriam and need not be followed. Conclusion: The decisions were made per incuriam and need not be followed, so the Court of Appeal is not bound to follow the earlier decision against Samuel.

items.stem: Samuel was convicted in the Crown Court. The Court of Appeal dismissed Samuel's appeal, applying an old Supreme Court precedent. The Supreme Court has now given permission to appeal and is asked to quash the conviction because the old precedent was wrongly decided. (a) Identify the main legal issue raised by these facts. (b) Explain how the Supreme Court could change the law and the outcome of Samuel's case.
items.answer: (a) Reversing and overruling. (b) Law: reversing: a higher court changes the decision of a lower court in the same case on appeal (Sweet v Parsley); overruling: the Supreme Court can overrule its own earlier decision using the Practice Statement 1966 (Herrington; R v G); overruling operates retrospectively. Application: by allowing Samuel's appeal the Supreme Court would reverse the Court of Appeal's decision; if it decides the old precedent was wrong it would overrule it; the Court of Appeal had to apply the old precedent because it was bound by it. Conclusion: The Supreme Court can both reverse the decision in Samuel's case and overrule the old precedent under the Practice Statement.

items.stem: In the context of the doctrine of precedent, identify and briefly explain one argument against the current law or system.
items.answer: Rigidity: bad decisions may stand for years (Addie v Dumbreck).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: valid point, e.g. rigidity: bad decisions may stand for years (Addie v Dumbreck); complexity and volume of case law; slow development, depending on appeals; retrospective effect (R v R; SW v UK); judicial law-making is undemocratic. 1 mark: brief explanation. [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of the doctrine of judicial precedent. Your answer should consider arguments on both sides and reach a conclusion.
items.answer: For: certainty and predictability; consistency and fairness; flexibility through distinguishing and the Practice Statement; detailed practical rules from real cases. Against: rigidity: bad decisions may stand for years (Addie v Dumbreck); complexity and volume of case law; slow development, depending on appeals; retrospective effect (R v R; SW v UK); judicial law-making is undemocratic. Conclusion: Precedent achieves a reasonable balance between certainty and flexibility, although it can be slow and rigid.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge and understanding [3]: accurate explanation of the law with supporting authority, e.g. British Railways Board v Herrington (1972); Balfour v Balfour and Merritt v Merritt; R v R (1991); SW v UK (1995); Young v Bristol Aeroplane (1944). AO3 Analysis and evaluation [5]: arguments supporting the view, e.g. certainty and predictability; consistency and fairness; flexibility through distinguishing and the Practice Statement; detailed practical rules from real cases; arguments against / problems, e.g. rigidity: bad decisions may stand for years (Addie v Dumbreck); complexity and volume of case law; slow development, depending on appeals; retrospective effect (R v R; SW v UK); judicial law-making is undemocratic. items.stem: Explain two points that could be used in answering the question: ""Judges should not make law." Discuss in the context of judicial precedent."
items.answer: judges are unelected, so law-making should be left to Parliament; retrospective effect of judge-made law is unfair; judges lack the resources for wide consultation.
items.markingKey: Per point: 1 mark identification, 1 mark development with authority. Points include: judges are unelected, so law-making should be left to Parliament; retrospective effect of judge-made law is unfair; judges lack the resources for wide consultation; judges must develop the law when Parliament has not acted (R v R; Donoghue v Stevenson); judge-made law can respond quickly to individual cases; Parliament can always reverse judicial decisions. [4]

items.stem: State what is meant by 'stare decisis'.
items.answer: Latin for "stand by what has been decided": the principle that courts follow the legal rules decided in earlier cases where the material facts are similar.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: basic/partial definition; 2 marks: full and accurate definition, i.e. latin for "stand by what has been decided": the principle that courts follow the legal rules decided in earlier cases where the material facts are similar. [2]

items.stem: Explain two sources of persuasive precedent.
items.answer: Obiter dicta (e.g. R v Howe followed in R v Gotts); decisions of lower courts or the Privy Council (A-G for Jersey v Holley); dissenting judgments (Candler v Crane Christmas); decisions of courts in other common law countries.
items.markingKey: 2 × (1 mark source, 1 mark example/explanation). [4]

items.stem: Explain why it can be difficult to identify the ratio decidendi of a case.
items.answer: Judges do not label the ratio; judgments can be long; in appeal courts each judge may give different reasons, so there may be no single ratio.

items.stem: Evaluate the importance of the distinction between ratio decidendi and obiter dicta in the doctrine of precedent. Your answer should consider arguments on both sides and reach a conclusion.
items.answer: For: only the ratio binds, so the law develops in a controlled way; obiter allows judges to signal future developments (High Trees, R v Howe); persuasive precedent gives flexibility. items.stem: State what is meant by 'Practice Statement 1966'.
items.answer: A statement by the Lord Chancellor on behalf of the House of Lords that it would treat its own former decisions as normally binding but would depart from them "when it appears right to do so"; it now applies to the Supreme Court.

items.stem: Explain the three exceptions in Young v Bristol Aeroplane Co (1944).
items.answer: The Court of Appeal may depart from its own decision where there are two conflicting decisions of its own (it must choose one); where its decision conflicts with a later House of Lords/Supreme Court decision; and where the decision was made per incuriam.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per exception. [3]

items.stem: Freya is a party to a case in the Court of Appeal (Civil Division). Advise Freya whether the Court of Appeal (Civil Division) must follow Rana v Coastline plc (fictional, 1998).
items.answer: Law: stare decisis: lower courts are bound by the ratio of higher courts; the Court of Appeal (Civil Division) is bound by its own decisions subject to the exceptions in Young v Bristol Aeroplane, and by the Supreme Court; Practice Statement 1966 used in Herrington (1972) and R v G (2003); Young v Bristol Aeroplane exceptions (1944); the court may also be able to distinguish the earlier case on its material facts. Application: the earlier decision was made by the Court of Appeal; the Court of Appeal (Civil Division) is bound by its own decisions subject to the exceptions in Young v Bristol Aeroplane, and by the Supreme Court; if the material facts differ, the Court of Appeal (Civil Division) could distinguish Rana v Coastline plc (fictional, 1998). Conclusion: Whether Rana v Coastline plc (fictional, 1998) must be followed depends on where the Court of Appeal sits in relation to the Court of Appeal (Civil Division); distinguishing may be possible if the material facts differ.

items.stem: In Green v Hollis (fictional, 2005), a higher court held that a promise between friends to share petrol costs was not legally binding. Sipho now brings a similar case in a lower court, but in Sipho's case the parties in Sipho's case had signed a written agreement and were running a business together. Explain how the lower court could avoid following Green v Hollis (fictional, 2005) and whether it is likely to do so. Explain the relevant legal rules before applying them.
items.answer: Law: a lower court is bound by the ratio of a higher court where the material facts are similar; it may distinguish the precedent if the material facts are significantly different (Balfour v Balfour and Merritt v Merritt); a lower court cannot overrule a higher court. Application: in Green v Hollis (fictional, 2005) the court held that a promise between friends to share petrol costs was not legally binding; in Sipho's case the parties in Sipho's case had signed a written agreement and were running a business together; this is a material difference, so the lower court can distinguish Green v Hollis (fictional, 2005). Conclusion: The lower court is likely to distinguish Green v Hollis (fictional, 2005) because the material facts differ, so it is not bound to follow it.

items.stem: Define the term 'overruling'.
items.answer: Where a higher court (or the Supreme Court under the Practice Statement) decides that the legal rule in an earlier case was wrong and sets it aside for the future.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: basic/partial definition; 2 marks: full and accurate definition, i.e. where a higher court (or the Supreme Court under the Practice Statement) decides that the legal rule in an earlier case was wrong and sets it aside for the future. [2]

items.stem: Explain two differences between distinguishing and overruling.
items.answer: Distinguishing leaves the earlier precedent intact while overruling sets it aside. Any court can distinguish but only a higher court (or the Supreme Court under the Practice Statement) can overrule.
items.markingKey: 2 × (1 mark identifies difference, 1 mark explains both sides). Valid differences include: distinguishing leaves the earlier precedent intact while overruling sets it aside; any court can distinguish but only a higher court (or the Supreme Court under the Practice Statement) can overrule; distinguishing depends on different material facts, overruling on the earlier law being wrong. items.stem: In Green v Hollis (fictional, 2005), a higher court held that a promise between friends to share petrol costs was not legally binding. Tomás now brings a similar case in a lower court, but in Tomás's case the parties in Tomás's case had signed a written agreement and were running a business together. Identify the main legal issue raised and state the relevant legal rule.
items.answer: Distinguishing a precedent. A lower court is bound by the ratio of a higher court where the material facts are similar.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies distinguishing a precedent. 1 mark: states the rule correctly, e.g. a lower court is bound by the ratio of a higher court where the material facts are similar. [2]

items.stem: Ravi was convicted in the Crown Court. The Court of Appeal dismissed Ravi's appeal, applying an old Supreme Court precedent. The Supreme Court has now given permission to appeal and is asked to quash the conviction because the old precedent was wrongly decided. Explain how the Supreme Court could change the law and the outcome of Ravi's case. Explain the relevant legal rules before applying them.
items.answer: Law: reversing: a higher court changes the decision of a lower court in the same case on appeal (Sweet v Parsley); overruling: the Supreme Court can overrule its own earlier decision using the Practice Statement 1966 (Herrington; R v G); overruling operates retrospectively. Application: by allowing Ravi's appeal the Supreme Court would reverse the Court of Appeal's decision; if it decides the old precedent was wrong it would overrule it; the Court of Appeal had to apply the old precedent because it was bound by it. Conclusion: The Supreme Court can both reverse the decision in Ravi's case and overrule the old precedent under the Practice Statement.

items.stem: In Green v Hollis (fictional, 2005), a higher court held that a shop was not liable for a customer's fall on a dry floor. Ethan now brings a similar case in a lower court, but in Ethan's case the floor in Ethan's case had been wet for two hours without a warning sign. (a) Identify the main legal issue raised by these facts. (b) Explain the relevant legal rules, referring to decided cases.
items.answer: (a) Distinguishing a precedent. (b) a lower court is bound by the ratio of a higher court where the material facts are similar; it may distinguish the precedent if the material facts are significantly different (Balfour v Balfour and Merritt v Merritt); a lower court cannot overrule a higher court.

items.stem: Briefly explain the legal principle established in SW v United Kingdom (1995).
items.answer: Facts: a husband convicted after R v R abolished the marital rape exemption argued that the law had been changed retrospectively. Principle: The European Court of Human Rights held there was no breach of Article 7 because the development of the law was reasonably foreseeable.

items.stem: Explain two disadvantages of the doctrine of precedent.
items.answer: Rigidity: lower courts must follow bad decisions; complexity and volume of reported cases; slow growth because change depends on cases being appealed; retrospective effect (R v R); judge-made law is undemocratic.
items.markingKey: 2 × (1 mark disadvantage, 1 mark explanation). [4]

items.stem: The Court of Appeal (Civil Division) is hearing an appeal by Ana. There are two earlier Court of Appeal decisions on the same point which conflict with a later Supreme Court decision. State, with a brief reason, the most likely legal outcome.
items.answer: The court must follow the Supreme Court decision, so the Court of Appeal is not bound to follow the earlier decision against Ana. Reason: the Court of Appeal is normally bound by its own previous decisions (Davis v Johnson 1979)
